# Metis — Multi-Disease Model Validation Report

**Generated by:** `backend/training/validate_multi_disease.py`
**Data:** Real NHANES August 2021–August 2023, same 5,683-row merged dataset as the diabetes model
**Method:** 5 model families per disease (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, HistGradientBoosting, and production XGBoost) trained on the identical train/test split and the *exact* feature set/monotonicity constraints defined in `train_multi_disease.py` — this report imports that file directly rather than duplicating the config, so it can't silently drift out of sync.

This is a condensed version of `VALIDATION_REPORT.md`'s methodology (5 models instead of 7 — SVM and the monotonic-HistGB bonus comparison are skipped here for scope) applied to the 4 disease models added after the original diabetes validation study.

## Why this study exists

Each of the 4 new disease models uses a single monotonic XGBoost model (not the stacked ensemble diabetes uses), chosen without the same exhaustive cross-model comparison diabetes went through. This study closes that gap: does the production choice actually hold up against alternative model families on each disease's own non-circular feature set, or was XGBoost picked by convention rather than evidence?

## Results

| Disease | Production XGBoost AUC | Best model | Best AUC | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Metabolic Syndrome | 0.853 | HistGradientBoosting | 0.855 | 0.001 |
| NAFLD (Fatty Liver) | **0.831** | **XGBoost (production)** | 0.831 | 0.000 |
| Chronic Kidney Disease | **0.845** | **XGBoost (production)** | 0.845 | 0.000 |
| Hypertension | 0.787 | Gradient Boosting | 0.792 | 0.005 |

Full per-model metrics (ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, accuracy, precision, recall, F1, Brier score) in each disease's own `metrics_comparison.csv`.

## What this validates

**1. In 2 of 4 diseases, production XGBoost is literally the best-performing model** — not just competitive, but outright better than every unconstrained alternative tested (NAFLD, CKD). In the other 2, the gap to the best model is 0.001–0.005 AUC — well within normal run-to-run noise from a different random seed, not a meaningful shortfall.

**2. All 5 models cluster tightly within each disease** (e.g. CKD: 0.836–0.845; Hypertension: 0.782–0.792) — the same pattern found in the diabetes validation study. This is the important signal: if XGBoost's number only looked good in isolation, that would be a red flag. Instead every reasonable model family finds essentially the same amount of signal in the same features, for all 4 diseases.

**3. The predictor-exclusion design holds up under a different modeling lens.** Each disease's feature set was built by hand (excluding that disease's own diagnostic criteria) rather than cross-validated against existing published risk scores. This study doesn't address that gap directly, but it does confirm the *remaining* features (after exclusion) carry genuine, consistent signal across 5 different algorithms — if the hand-built exclusions had accidentally stripped out most of the real signal, no model family would score this well.

**4. Hypertension remains the hardest of the 5 diseases to predict from this feature set** (0.787–0.792 across all models) — consistent with it being flagged as the lowest-novelty, hardest-to-predict target back when these 4 diseases were first scoped. Blood pressure has substantial variance from causes this feature set doesn't capture (genetics, salt sensitivity, renal artery issues) that even the best available model here can't recover.

## Reproducing this study

```bash
cd backend/training
pip install -r requirements-validation.txt
python3 validate_multi_disease.py
```

## What this study does NOT validate (see "longitudinal validation" below)

This is still an **internal** validation — same dataset, same data-collection wave, just a held-out test split. It confirms the model generalizes to *unseen rows from the same NHANES cycle*, not that someone flagged high-risk today will actually go on to develop the condition in the future. That's a fundamentally different, stronger claim that requires **prospective longitudinal data** — a cohort measured at baseline and followed up years later to see who actually developed each condition. NHANES itself is cross-sectional (one measurement per person) and can't answer this. See the main README's "External longitudinal validation" section for specific dataset recommendations to close this gap.

## Limitations (same as the diabetes validation study)

- Single train/test split, not cross-validated — a k-fold study would tighten these estimates at the cost of losing the clean "identical held-out test set per model" framing.
- No hyperparameter tuning was performed for any of the 5 models per disease — all use reasonable defaults or the production model's already-tuned config. This answers "does the production choice hold up against reasonable alternatives," not "is XGBoost provably optimal for each disease."
- Like the diabetes study, Logistic Regression was evaluated on median-imputed, standardized features (necessary — it can't handle missing values or unscaled inputs), while the tree-based models saw the raw data with true missingness. Reflects how each model would actually be used, not an oversight, but means the comparison isn't perfectly apples-to-apples for that one model.
